content: The process of assessing the risk of bias in studies involves numerous subjective judgments, particularly when published papers lack detailed information. To address this, disagreements among authors were resolved through mutual discussion. If any author was unable to comment on the risk of bias due to insufficient information, the risk was categorized as uncertain. Given the large number of studies included in the review and the significant time gap between the conduct of most studies and this review, it was practically challenging to contact study authors for additional information. To minimize the risk of publication bias, efforts were made to search for grey literature, trial registries, and references from included studies and other systematic reviews. However, unpublished data stored in government or non-government agency files or electronic records, which are not publicly available, may still have been missed. Despite employing a broad search strategy, it is possible that studies reporting relevant exposures and outcomes in the full text, but not explicitly mentioning breastfeeding in the title or abstract, were overlooked. Language bias was minimized by not restricting searches to any specific language and by translating abstracts or full texts into English when necessary. Our review primarily focused on the effects of continued breastfeeding beyond one year compared to breastfeeding for at least 6–12 months (median of 9 months or range of 6–12 months). Studies that did not report comparative data were excluded, unlike other systematic reviews that assessed breastfeeding into the second year against no breastfeeding or shorter durations (<6 months). However, many studies provided estimates for breastfeeding into the second year compared to shorter durations (e.g., no breastfeeding or <6 months) and also provided similar estimates for our control group (6–12 months or 9–12 months). This allowed us to calculate summary estimates relevant to our objectives. Our findings, based on a larger study base, suggested a trend toward reduced overweight/obesity with prolonged breastfeeding beyond one year, particularly in lowand middle-income countries (LMICs). A review by Zeng (2020) summarized evidence linking breastfeeding with a reduced risk of attention deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) in children. This review included 12 studies (cohort, case-control, and cross-sectional) with 3,686 ADHD cases among 106,907 children. Four studies compared ADHD prevalence in children breastfed for over 12 months versus less than 12 months. Sensitivity analysis showed that excluding two studies with a high risk of bias resulted in a lack of statistical significance. A systematic review by Sankar (2015) evaluated the effects of breastfeeding on all-cause and infection-related mortality in children aged 6–23 months. Of the 13 included studies, data were drawn from various countries, including Bangladesh, India, Ghana, and others. The review found a higher risk of all-cause mortality in children aged 6–11 months and 12–23 months who were not breastfed compared to those breastfed for any duration. However, the quality of evidence was very low to low for comparisons of no breastfeeding versus any breastfeeding at 6–23 months. While this review suggested an association between breastfeeding and reduced child mortality, it did not specifically address the impact of breastfeeding beyond one year compared to shorter durations. A meta-analysis from China (Cui, 2017) evaluated the association between breastfeeding duration and early childhood caries (ECC). The authors concluded that while breastfeeding may protect against ECC, breastfeeding beyond 12 months could increase the risk compared to breastfeeding for less than 12 months, with high heterogeneity among studies. Most included studies were of low quality. Our review also suggested a slightly higher association of prolonged breastfeeding with caries, but the estimates were not directly comparable as Cui (2017) considered any shorter duration of breastfeeding as the comparison group. A review by the Collaborative Group on Hormonal Factors in Breast Cancer (2002) analyzed data from 47 epidemiological studies across 30 countries, involving 50,302 women with invasive breast cancer and 96,973 controls. The authors reported a 4.3% reduction in breast cancer risk for every 12 months of breastfeeding, concluding that longer breastfeeding duration provides greater protection. However, uncertainty remains about the magnitude of this protective effect due to inaccuracies in reported lifetime breastfeeding duration, often rounded to multiples of 6 or 12 months. A pooled analysis of 13 case-control studies (Babic, 2020) examined the association between breastfeeding duration and ovarian cancer risk by histotype. The analysis suggested that longer breastfeeding duration was protective against ovarian cancer, but the comparison was limited to no breastfeeding and not directly comparable to our estimates. Similarly, a systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis (Aune, 2014) found a 9% reduction in type 2 diabetes risk for every 12-month increase in lifetime breastfeeding duration. Study quality was relatively high, but the population was heterogeneous, including women with gestational diabetes, American nurses, and women from the general population. A systematic review (Torris, 2020) analyzed the association between lactation duration and metabolic syndrome (MetS) in women. Seven of the ten included studies suggested that breastfeeding might prevent or improve metabolic health and play a protective role in MetS prevention. However, the pooled effect was inconclusive, and most studies were limited by design (80% cross-sectional) with moderate methodological quality. A meta-analysis (Xiao, 2020) investigating the association between breastfeeding and osteoporotic hip fractures included seven studies (two cohort and five case-control) with 103,898 subjects. The analysis demonstrated that the incidence of osteoporotic hip fractures decreased with longer breastfeeding duration. All studies were of moderate or high quality with no significant heterogeneity. Exclusive breastfeeding for the first six months is an established, effective, and safe child survival intervention, and global efforts to promote it are ongoing. This review suggests that continued breastfeeding into the second year may not offer significant advantages or disadvantages in terms of child health (e.g., neurodevelopment, anthropometry, infectious morbidity, cardiometabolic health) or maternal health (e.g., cancer, cardiometabolic health, bone health) compared to stopping before one year. In LMICs, continued breastfeeding into the second year may be associated with lower odds of obesity/overweight without increasing the risk of undernutrition. However, there may be a slightly higher risk of dental caries in children breastfed beyond one year, necessitating proper oral hygiene measures. Given the very low certainty of evidence, further research is likely to change the direction and magnitude of these estimates. Research gaps include the need for national-level breastfeeding duration data registries, large-scale randomized trials, and well-designed cohort studies to evaluate the shortand medium-term benefits of breastfeeding beyond one year. Additionally, data from LMICs on child and maternal outcomes, such as infectious morbidity, asthma, cancer, and cardiometabolic health, are lacking and require further investigation.
